Yes — one thing upstream genuinely required fixing, and it's the most consequential defect found in this project so far.

## P1 was never person-disjoint

The shards store **video ids** as `subjects`. That decision rests on a claim recorded in `docs/07_kaggle_plan.md`: *"Charades subject ids do not exist publicly."*

**That claim is false.** [`Charades_v1_train.csv` has carried a `subject` column all along](https://prior.allenai.org/projects/data/charades/README.txt) — a unique id for each of the **267 actors**, ~30 videos each. At that ratio, a video-id split puts essentially every *person* on both sides. Same actor, same home, same mannerisms in train and val. The disjointness assertion could never catch it, because the ids really are disjoint — it's the people behind them that aren't.

The sharpest irony: `subject_from_path()` was built to prevent *exactly this* in the fall corpora ("the ids are disjoint — the PEOPLE behind them are not," GMDCSA's `Subject 1/01.mp4` vs `Subject 2/01.mp4`). We committed the same failure on the biggest corpus, and the CSV that fixes it is already inside `charades-480p`, attached to every session.

**What this means for the numbers:** every P1 figure to date is video-disjoint, not person-disjoint, and likely optimistic. The fall head is less affected (its corpora already use real people, plus ADL negatives), but the ADL mean-class/macro-F1 numbers need the caveat — now written into `results/evaluation.md` and the README limitations, ahead of anyone else spotting it.

**The fix, all in place and tested (166/166, full suite including training):**
- `load_subject_map()` / `remap_subjects()` — video→actor remap, applied at *split time only*; shards keep video ids, which sequence reconstruction still needs. Non-Charades ids pass through, coverage is reported, <50% coverage refuses to train.
- `train_adl.py --subject-map`, notebook 03 passes it automatically when the CSV is present, notebook 04 auto-detects it and prints the split mode next to P1.
- **Resume guard extended**: a checkpoint trained under one split identity is refused under the other — resuming across identities would smuggle the old boundary's leakage into the new protocol. (Also added `sampler`/`tau_train` to that guard while there.)
- **S13** proves it: on a Charades-shaped fixture, the video-id split leaks 4 of 5 actors onto both sides; the actor-id split leaks zero. Positive control included, so the assertion can't pass vacuously.

## What I audited and found sound

Slot tracking (S8), the best-covering window labelling, fall labelling by true frame position, `normalise()` dropout handling, bone flip equivariance, the MMDetection-free preflight — all already regression-tested against the failures they once had. The remaining known upstream issue is the **`walking` label-map audit** (563 windows, 1.7% — implausible), which is a data question for `charades_map_review.tsv`, not a code fix.

## Consequence for the plan

This changes the retraining calculus from my earlier advice. Before: "retraining is optional, try post-hoc levers first." Now: **one notebook-03 retrain is required** for defensible P1 numbers — the current checkpoints measure a protocol we can no longer claim. Expect the person-disjoint numbers to come out *lower*; that's not a regression, it's the honest measurement.

| Component | Number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|

Context for the ADL judgment: many of your classes are **object-defined, not pose-defined**. Drinking, eating, and taking_medication are nearly identical skeletons — hand to mouth while seated. Reading vs using_phone vs watching_tv is the same slouch. No amount of ST-GCN capacity recovers information the input modality discards, and your per-class F1 table shows exactly this: pose-defined classes (lying_down, sitting) do fine, object-defined ones sit at 0.07–0.20. Charades RGB models score ~40–45 mAP *with* appearance; skeleton-only, per-window, on a remapped 18-class taxonomy, 0.375 top-1 is not embarrassing. It's just not sufficient alone.

## Where the leverage is, in rough order of expected return

**1. The missing NTU pretrain — probably your single biggest lever.** Preflight has been warning `MISSING stgcnpp_ntu60_joint.pth` the whole time, meaning all four streams trained from scratch on ~126k windows. NTU-60 pretraining typically buys skeleton models 5–15 points on downstream ADL tasks, and it directly addresses your other symptom: peaks at epoch 3–9 then decay is a from-scratch model overfitting fast. Get that checkpoint staged and rerun notebook 03. Cheapest high-value change available.

**2. Feed RT-DETR object context into Agent 2.** You already run RT-DETR in the pipeline. A tiny fusion — concatenate "cup/phone/book/vacuum detected near hands" as a per-window feature vector, or a late-fusion logit bias — attacks exactly the confusions skeleton can't resolve. Your own second-person experiment is proof of concept: one binary context bit took class-18 recall from 0.060 to 0.148. Objects should do far more, because more classes are object-defined than person-defined.

**3. Fix the fall head's negatives, not its architecture.** Val AUROC 1.000 means your negatives are trivially separable — the model can cheat. Three concrete moves:
- **Hard negatives**: mine sitting_down, lying_down, bending_reaching windows from the ADL shards (you have them labeled!) and inject them as fall-negatives. These are the true confusers.
- **Leave-one-dataset-out training**: you have four fall datasets; train on three, validate on the fourth, rotate. That makes cross-dataset AUROC your *selection* metric instead of a post-hoc surprise.
- **Normalization audit**: below-chance AUROC on GMDCSA (0.471) smells like a preprocessing mismatch (skeleton scale, camera height, coordinate convention) rather than pure generalization failure. Worth an hour of eyeballing before any retraining.

**4. Gate the reporter with the verifier you already built.** C1–C4 is deterministic and cheap — run it at *inference* time and suppress or regenerate failed claims instead of only scoring them offline. That turns 8% hallucination into ~0% delivered hallucination, and the dissertation framing improves from "the model hallucinates 8%" to "the system delivers verified claims; the verifier catches 8% pre-delivery." Given your grammar result (no faithfulness gain, 7.4× cost), verifier-gated free decoding is arguably the headline architecture.

**5. Smaller items, roughly in order:**
- **Class-balanced training** (balanced sampler or logit-adjusted *loss*, not just post-hoc τ) — other_idle is 41% of val and post-hoc adjustment already buys +0.063, so baking it into training should do at least as well without the top-1 collapse.
- **Ensemble weighting**: bone alone beats the 4-stream logit-average on mean-class (0.187 vs 0.156); the motion streams are diluting it. A weighted or 2-stream ensemble is a free win.
- **Label-map cleanup**: `charades_map_review.tsv` exists — a pass over the noisiest verb mappings (cleaning_housework, personal_hygiene are big classes with low F1) may be part label noise, not model error.
- **Skeleton augmentation** (random rotation, scale, joint dropout) to push the peak epoch later.

**The leak was buying precision, not recall.** Mean-class barely moved (0.152 → 0.156) but **macro-F1 fell 0.152 → 0.128** and F1≥50 fell 0.161 → 0.136. Only reporting both metrics made that visible — a mean-class-only writeup would have concluded "the leak didn't matter."

**The per-class table is the strongest evidence in the project that the fix mattered.** Habit-and-context classes collapsed while pose-defined classes *improved*:

| class | video-disj. | person-disj. |
|---|---|---|
| `cleaning_housework` | 0.193 | **0.098** |
| `personal_hygiene` | 0.176 | **0.074** |
| `eating` | 0.164 | **0.082** |
| `lying_down` | 0.408 | **0.435** |
| `sitting` | 0.318 | **0.341** |

That contrast is exactly what a model looks like when it stops recognising *the person* and starts recognising *the posture*. Invisible in any aggregate.

**The fragmentation column changed the deployment answer** — which is why it was added. `argmax + logit-adjust` wins mean-class at 0.209 and fragments **3.32×**; deploying it would report ~3× the true `walking_bouts` at a third of the true mean duration while looking best in the accuracy column. `Viterbi fitted + logit-adjust` (0.194 mean-class, frag 0.62) is the only row defensible on both axes, and neither column would have picked it alone.

**Second-person context worked exactly where aimed**: class-18 recall 0.060 → 0.148 at unchanged precision (F1 0.047 → 0.058), 7.5% of windows, small global cost. Worth deploying because it feeds the social-withdrawal alert — not as a general lever.

## What it does

A new **On your own footage** band takes a clip and runs Agents 1 and 2 on it. RTMO extracts COCO-17 poses for every person in shot, the tracker holds an identity across frames, OSNet decides which one is the resident, and the ST-GCN++ ensemble labels each person's activity on their own windows. The skeletons are drawn back over the playing video from the coordinates the model returned, with one timeline per person and fall segments struck in pencil.

Verified in the browser: two people tracked, resident's row showing `walking 3.0s · standing 2.0s · falling 1.0s · fallen_on_ground 3.9s` with the two fall segments in pencil and `peak fall posterior 0.71`; the visitor's row showing `walking 4.5s · interacting_with_person 5.4s` with none. Both timelines are scaled to the *clip's* span rather than each track's, so they line up and can be compared — the point of an identity-aware system.

## Three things I made sure of rather than assumed

**The coordinate mapping.** This is the one thing in an overlay that fails silently: wrong scale draws a plausible skeleton floating beside the person. I forced a 640 px element over a 1280 px source and sampled canvas pixels — ink at the shoulder, bone midpoint and elbow, nothing at the empty regions, and **nothing at the position an unscaled draw would have used**. That last check is what makes the first three mean something.

**The crash boundary.** Decode runs in a child process, and that isn't defensive habit. cv2 delegates to ffmpeg, ffmpeg raises SIGSEGV on malformed streams, and a signal is not an exception — `try/except` cannot see it and the interpreter stops. Notebook 02 lost finished corpora to exactly this. Inline, one bad upload would kill the kernel, the tunnel and the demo together. Test P16 confirms a failing child becomes a `ValueError` while the parent stays alive, and `crash_reason` handles both POSIX negative codes and Windows' NTSTATUS — a bare `returncode < 0` is right on Kaggle and wrong on the machine the tests run on.

**The wire format round-trip.** `rebuild_observations` is the only thing that reads the compact format back, so P16 pushes two wire people through `frames_to_windows` and asserts **two** window sets come out in `[N,30,2,17,3]`. If that drifts, two people silently arrive as one.

## Two design calls worth flagging

**Identity is weight and fill, not colour.** The palette has three hues and each already means something — ink verified, pencil a correction, ochre "watch this". ## Architecture — four agents, one boundary

```
video ──► AGENT 1  RTMO pose ──► tracker ──► OSNet re-ID ──► role
                                                              │

                                     │
          AGENT 4  Qwen2.5-7B, schema-constrained ──► Claims
                   ──► DETERMINISTIC VERIFIER ──► verified report
```

Agents don't call each other. They hand over **versioned Pydantic schemas persisted to SQLite**, so every stage is independently testable and replayable — Agent 3 and 4 re-run in seconds without touching video.

**The load-bearing boundary:** the LLM receives structured state only. That's what makes the auditability claim mean anything.

## The contribution

Every claim must carry a machine-resolvable `evidence_ref`, then passes four checks that use **no LLM at all** (a model checking a model shares its blind spots):

| Check | Catches |
|---|---|
| C1 `ref_exists` | fabricated citations |
| C2 `value_matches` | invented numbers |
| C3 `pct_matches` | wrong percentages |
| C4 `direction_consistent` | **inverted narration** — right number, backwards story |

| | what it does | mode |
|---|---|---|
| 00 / 01a | stage wheels, ONNX weights, Charades | online |
| 01 | Charades → skeleton shards (**165,109 windows / 7,985 videos**) | offline |
| 02 | 4 fall corpora → shards (**3,064 windows**) | online |
| 03 | train 4 ADL streams + fall head | offline, Blackwell |
| 04 | P1 / P2 / levers / segments / Agent 4 table | offline, Blackwell |
| 05 | serve the models behind a Cloudflare tunnel | online, T4/P100 |

Training notebooks have **no internet**, so every asset must already exist in an attached dataset. Every notebook resolves mounts by *content*, never by dataset name, and a repo contract (22 tokens) fails at cell 1 if the code snapshot is stale.

## Front end

## The biggest thing you found, but not the way you framed it

**Item 6's premise is false: P2 was never measuring the fall head.** The cell does `post = softmax(clf.logits(Xh))` where `clf` is the 4-stream **ADL ensemble**, then sums classes 7+8. `runs/fall/best.pt` is never loaded in notebook 04. So 0.471–0.603 is the ADL ensemble's fall-class transfer; the dedicated head's 0.822 AUPRC comes from `train_fall.py`'s own internal val split and **has never been evaluated leave-one-dataset-out at all.**

My own `evaluation.md` prose repeated that conflation — "read together with the fall head's own numbers… 0.822 is an in-domain ceiling" — which was my error. P2 now loads the real head (reads `stream` from the checkpoint rather than assuming, strips the `net.` prefix, `ravel()`s the single logit) and reports **both** columns side by side. The harness fixture gained a `FallHead`-shaped checkpoint so that branch actually executes — without it, it printed `nan` and passed vacuously.

So items 6a/6b (domain-adversarial, mixup) are premature: we don't yet know what we'd be fixing. One notebook-04 run tells us.

## Item 4 conflicts with item 3, and I fixed both together

T=0.63 was fitted on the **4-stream ensemble's** logits. Deploying `bone` alone with 0.63 would be miscalibrated — and Viterbi and abstention both consume those posteriors. Hardcoding any number is the bug; the number just happened to be stale too.

Notebook 05 now sets `STREAMS = ("bone",)`, loads only those checkpoints (`from_run_dir` was pulling in all four by accident), and **refits T from `val_logits.npz` for the streams actually served** — free, on CPU. No `val_logits.npz` attached → T=1.0 with a loud warning rather than a plausible wrong number.

## Item 2: implemented as a diagnostic, and it confirms your hypothesis

I did **not** add locomotion regexes. I don't have the real 157-class list here, and a wrong rule teaches a wrong label then costs a ~6-hour re-extraction to undo. Instead `build_charades_map.py` now groups the fallback by candidate theme. On a realistic slice it immediately flags:

```
locomotion?      4 class(es)
                 c010 Going to a room
                 c011 Leaving a room
                 c012 Entering a room through a doorway
                 c013 Going upstairs
```

Run it against the real `Charades_v1_classes.txt` and you'll see the true count in one CPU second. N8 asserts the probe fires **and** that none of those classes got auto-assigned.

One correction to your framing: this is not "the cheapest data fix." Labels are baked into shards at extraction — the shard stores taxonomy ids, not Charades action ids — so changing `RULES` means re-extracting 165,109 windows (~6 h) *and* retraining. Cheap to decide, expensive to apply. The audit exists so you decide once.

## Item 1: RT-DETR cannot improve any number we can measure

The ADL shards contain skeletons only — `[N,T,M,17,3]`, no pixels, no object array. At evaluation time `fuse_objects()` would receive `()` for every window whether or not a detector exists, **because there are no frames to run it on.** So the claim that it "would change `taking_medication`'s F1 floor from 0.072 to something meaningful" is not verifiable: activating it requires re-extraction with RT-DETR at 1 Hz plus a shard-format change plus retraining, on top of the walking-map re-extraction.

At *serving* time (notebook 05, real video) a detector would genuinely work — and its benefit would be unmeasurable under our current protocol. That's worth building as a serving feature with that caveat stated, not as an accuracy claim. Your evidence from the second-person experiment is real but it's precisely the signal that *didn't* need a detector, because the tracker had already recorded it in slot 1.

We have no cooking-decline scenario in the simulator, so the threshold would be invented. That's how the 67.66 false-alerts-per-100-days regression happened.

One job, four stage payloads, keyed **per track** so multiple people fall out naturally — a single-person video is just the degenerate case with one track.

```python
    status: str                 # "done" | "skipped" | "failed"
    elapsed_s: float
    payload: dict

```

**Agent 1 — perception.** Per sampled frame: RTMO detections, track id, 17-keypoint skeletons, plus the ReID decision (which tracks merged into which person, and any open-set "unknown person" verdicts). Also emit a downsampled overlay JPEG every N frames — the website needs something visual here, not just arrays:

```python

    }
}
```

**Agent 2 — activity.** This is where the serving-config work you just did must surface. Per track, per window: the calibrated posteriors (refitted T, served `STREAMS`), the argmax label, the abstention flag (τ=0.25), then the Viterbi-smoothed segment list. Expose *both* raw windows and smoothed segments — the whole point of showing agent internals is letting a user see Viterbi correct a flicker:

```python
"payload": {
    "streams_served": ["bone"], "temperature": 0.71, "tau": 0.25,
    "per_track": {
        "track_0": {
            "windows": [{"t": 0.0, "top": "walking", "p": 0.81, "abstained": false}, ...],
            "segments": [{"label": "walking", "start": 0.0, "end": 14.2}, ...],
        }
    }
}
```

**Agent 3 — behavior.** Per person (post-ReID, not per track): the duration features including `lying_duration_s`, and any alert-rule evaluations with their thresholds shown, so the UI can display *why* an alert did or didn't fire.

**Agent 4 — verifier + reporter.** The verifier's per-token contract check (21/21 or the failing tokens listed) and the caregiver report text, per person. **Toyota's skeletons are 15-joint 3D, estimated from RGB — not COCO-17 2D.** From `graph/smarthome.py`: `num_node = 15`, 14 edges. Output `(N, 3, 4000, 15, 1)`.

Our pipeline is COCO-17 2D `[N,T,M,17,3]` with `(x, y, score)`. So there is **no clean remap**. Going 15→17 means inventing 2 joints we don't have and discarding the z-axis — throwing away information *and* fabricating some. Every COCO-17-dependent piece breaks: the adjacency, `FLIP_INDEX`, `to_bone()`'s parent map, and `normalise()`'s torso reference.

**The correct route is exactly the one I told you to skip.** Download the RGB, run *our* RTMO on it, and produce COCO-17 2D skeletons in our own format. Then Toyota windows are byte-identical in structure to Charades windows, every downstream component works unchanged, and the transfer result is honest — the same extractor on both populations, so any accuracy gap is the *population*, not a joint-format artifact.

Using their skeletons would confound the finding you actually want with a format change. That's not a minor accuracy risk; it's an uninterpretable experiment.

Cost on your hardware: 16,115 trimmed clips at ~1,333 videos/h (measured on Charades) ≈ **12 GPU-hours**, so 1–2 offline sessions. Well within budget, and it's the same notebook-01 code path.

Fair challenge — I asserted that without justifying it. The honest answer has three parts, and one of them is a real cost worth stating.

**Nothing in the pipeline consumes depth.** RTMO takes RGB frames. `ObjectDetector` (RT-DETR) takes RGB. OSNet ReID takes RGB crops. The shard format is `[N,T,M,17,3]` where the 3 is `(x, y, score)` — a 2D pixel coordinate plus a confidence. There is no channel for a depth value and no consumer for one. So depth isn't "skipped for cost," it's currently unusable without new architecture.

**Depth is Toyota-only, which is what makes it dangerous rather than merely idle.** Charades has none. None of the four fall corpora has any. If we built a depth-consuming branch it would be trained on Toyota alone — and then the cross-population transfer result becomes uninterpretable, because the Toyota model would have an input modality the Charades model never had. The P4 finding you want ("trained on young adults, measured on real elderly") requires the *same* input format on both sides. That's the same reason I said to extract COCO-17 from Toyota's RGB rather than use their 15-joint skeletons.

**The real cost of my advice:** depth would genuinely help two known weaknesses, and I should have said so rather than dismissing it.

- `lying_down` vs `fallen_on_ground` is currently disambiguated "by onset velocity + location, not pose alone" (taxonomy note). Depth gives height-above-floor directly, which is the physically correct discriminator.
- Depth resolves the 2D projection ambiguity behind `sitting`/`standing` confusion when a camera is near eye level.

So it's a legitimate future direction, just not one that fits inside this project's remaining month or its cross-corpus protocol.

**Practical point:** if the download is cheap and your 30-day window is the binding constraint, take the depth anyway. Storage is reversible; a lapsed credential is not.
```python
# --- staged job model -------------------------------------------------------------
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pathlib import Path
import json, time, uuid, threading

JOBS = Path("/kaggle/working/jobs"); JOBS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
_JOBS: dict[str, dict] = {}
_LOCK = threading.Lock()

AGENTS = (("agent1_perception", "Agent 1 — detect, track, identify"),
          ("agent2_activity",   "Agent 2 — skeleton windows to activities"),
          ("agent3_behaviour",  "Agent 3 — daily features, baseline, alerts"),
          ("agent4_report",     "Agent 4 — constrained claims, then verified"))

class StageOutput(BaseModel):
    agent: str
    title: str
    status: str            # pending | running | done | skipped | failed
    elapsed_s: float = 0.0
    summary: str = ""
    payload: dict = {}

def _init_job(job_id: str, filename: str) -> dict:
    return {"job_id": job_id, "filename": filename, "created": time.time(),
            "n_people": 0, "tracks": [],
            "served": {"streams": list(STREAMS), "temperature": TEMPERATURE,
                       "tau": TAU, "decoding": "viterbi_fitted+logit_adjust"},
            "stages": [StageOutput(agent=a, title=t, status="pending").model_dump()
                       for a, t in AGENTS]}

def _set_stage(job_id: str, agent: str, **kw) -> None:
    with _LOCK:
        for s in _JOBS[job_id]["stages"]:
            if s["agent"] == agent:
                s.update(kw)
        (JOBS / job_id / "job.json").write_text(
            json.dumps(_JOBS[job_id], default=str), encoding="utf-8")
```

```python
@app.post("/video")
async def upload_video(file: UploadFile = File(...), x_token: str = Header(default="")):
    _auth(x_token)
    job_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]
    d = JOBS / job_id; d.mkdir(parents=True)
    raw = await file.read()
    if len(raw) > MAX_UPLOAD_MB * 1_000_000:
        raise HTTPException(413, f"max {MAX_UPLOAD_MB} MB")
    (d / "input.mp4").write_bytes(raw)
    with _LOCK:
        _JOBS[job_id] = _init_job(job_id, file.filename or "upload.mp4")
    threading.Thread(target=_run_pipeline, args=(job_id,), daemon=True).start()
    return {"job_id": job_id, "poll": f"/job/{job_id}"}

@app.get("/job/{job_id}")
def get_job(job_id: str):
    with _LOCK:
        job = _JOBS.get(job_id)
    if job is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, "unknown job")
```

The worker, with each agent's payload shaped for display:

```python
def _run_pipeline(job_id: str) -> None:
    d = JOBS / job_id
    try:
        # ---- Agent 1 -------------------------------------------------------------
        _set_stage(job_id, "agent1_perception", status="running")
        t0 = time.time()
        frames, stats = detect_and_track(str(d / "input.mp4"), fps_sample=FPS_SAMPLE,
                                        keyframe_dir=d)   # writes t<track>_<f>.jpg
        by_track = {}
        for fr in frames:
            for p in fr.persons:
                tr = by_track.setdefault(p.track_id, {
                    "track_id": p.track_id, "n_frames": 0, "role": p.role.value,
                    "role_confidence": p.role_confidence, "rooms": set(),
                    "keyframes": sorted(str(q.relative_to(JOBS))
                                        for q in d.glob(f"t{p.track_id}_*.jpg"))[:6]})
                tr["n_frames"] += 1
                if p.room: tr["rooms"].add(p.room)
        tracks = [{**t, "rooms": sorted(t["rooms"])} for t in by_track.values()]
        # Resident selection is SHOWN, never silent: two resident-ish tracks or none is a
        # real ambiguity and Agent 3 runs on exactly one subject.
        residents = [t for t in tracks if t["role"] == "resident"]
        chosen = max(residents or tracks, key=lambda t: t["n_frames"], default=None)
        _set_stage(job_id, "agent1_perception", status="done",
                   elapsed_s=round(time.time() - t0, 1),
                   summary=f"{len(tracks)} person track(s), {stats.frames} frames at "
                           f"{FPS_SAMPLE} fps",
                   payload={"fps_sampled": FPS_SAMPLE, "frames_read": stats.frames,
                            "tracks": tracks, "reid_tau": 0.355,
                            "resident_selection": {
                                "chosen_track": chosen and chosen["track_id"],
                                "method": "role==RESIDENT, longest track",
                                "ambiguous": len(residents) != 1},
                            "dropped": {"unusable_pose": stats.dropped_unusable,
                                        "short_tracks": stats.dropped_short}})

        # ---- Agent 2 -------------------------------------------------------------
        _set_stage(job_id, "agent2_activity", status="running")
        t0 = time.time(); per_track = {}
        for tr in tracks:
            windows, segs = classify_track(frames, tr["track_id"], STATE["clf"],
                                           temperature=TEMPERATURE, tau=TAU)
            per_track[str(tr["track_id"])] = {
                "n_windows": len(windows),
                "windows": [{"t0": w.t0, "t1": w.t1, "label": w.label_name,
                             "p": round(w.confidence, 3), "abstained": w.abstained}
                            for w in windows],
                "segments": [{"label": s.label_name, "start": s.start_s, "end": s.end_s,
                              "confidence": round(s.confidence, 3)} for s in segs]}
        _set_stage(job_id, "agent2_activity", status="done",
                   elapsed_s=round(time.time() - t0, 1),
                   summary=f"{sum(v['n_windows'] for v in per_track.values())} windows → "
                           f"{sum(len(v['segments']) for v in per_track.values())} segments "
                           f"across {len(per_track)} track(s)",
                   payload={"served": _JOBS[job_id]["served"], "per_track": per_track})
        # ... Agent 3 and Agent 4 follow the same shape
    except Exception as exc:
        _set_stage(job_id, _current_agent(job_id), status="failed",
                   summary=f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
```

## The staged website: implemented

`/video` now returns `stages[]` — one record per agent with `agent`, `name`, `status`, `elapsed_s`, `payload` — plus `checks[]` with C1–C4 **individually per claim**.

| stage | payload |
|---|---|
| 1 perception | fps, frames_kept, providers, `n_people`, reid, tracks with roles |
| 2 activity | streams_served, τ, T, decoding chain, per-track segments |
| 3 behaviour | `features_from_video` (real), deviations, alerts, `baseline_provenance`, caveats |
| 4 report | model, summary, recommendation, escalate, claim counts, hallucination rate |
| checks[] | text, evidence_ref, claimed_value, `C1_ref_exists`…`C4_direction_consistent`, notes, `shown_to_caregiver` |

Multi-person works because segments carry `track_id` and `role` — one person or several, same shape.

**Two real bugs surfaced doing it.** The endpoint was re-implementing Agent 2 as `logit_adjust → softmax → argmax → run-length`, which **skipped Viterbi smoothing and abstention entirely** — the served labels were not the configuration notebook 04 evaluated, so the demo would have shown numbers no table backs. It now runs through `ActivityPipeline` with an adapter that folds τ into `logits()`, so serving and evaluation are the same path. And Agents 3–4 were absent from the response altogether.

**The judgement call on Agent 3.** I did not fabricate a resident history. The baseline is a *declared* simulated reference, labelled on every affected number, with the distinction stated in the payload: feature **values** are measured from the video and are real; robust-z and alerts are **reference-relative**. C1–C4 still check each claim against the state computed from that video, so the verifier's guarantee is untouched — what a reference baseline cannot support is the clinical reading ("mobility declined"), and the response says so rather than leaving a reader to infer it.

## Toyota Smarthome: what the public pipelines show

- **16K RGB+D clips, 31 classes, real seniors, fully unscripted, 7 views.** Cross-subject uses 31 classes, cross-view 19.
- **Skeletons are pre-extracted and shipped** — your email lists v1.1 and refined v1.2; [UNIK](https://github.com/YangDi666/UNIK) uses v2.0 refined by SSTA-PRS. **No RTMO extraction needed**, which skips the 6.26 h that Charades cost.
- The headline metric is **mean per-class accuracy** — exactly our metric of record, so the numbers are comparable in kind rather than needing translation.
- UNIK gives exact configs (`config/smarthome-cross-subject/train_joint.yaml`, `train_bone.yaml`), a `smarthome_gendata.py` converter, `gen_bone_data.py`, an ensemble script, and separate `evaluation-cs.py` / `evaluation-cv.py` scorers. That maps almost 1:1 onto our joint/bone streams and logit-average ensemble.

**The caveat that matters.** [improved_HAR_on_Toyota](https://github.com/DAIGroup/improved_HAR_on_Toyota) reports **+9.5% cross-subject** from preprocessing — and the core of it is **rotation-normalising skeletons**. Our `normalise()` deliberately refuses that, and the docstring says why: a fallen person's orientation relative to gravity *is* the signal. Toyota has no fall class, so it's free there. We have classes 7/8 and the fall head is our strongest result — applying it globally would reproduce exactly the bug that scored AUROC 0.466. The correct design is a rotation-normalised **additional stream for the ADL head only**, never for the fall head, and S4b already exists to catch it if that boundary slips.

## What I'd do with the Blackwell, in order

1. **Convert Toyota skeletons to our shard format** (CPU, ~minutes) — 31 classes → our 20 via a reviewed map, same `charades_map_review.tsv` discipline, plus the built-in cross-subject split so we stop improvising actor ids.
2. **Train the four streams on Toyota** (one GPU session). This is the run that removes limitation 1 — reported accuracies stop being an upper bound on elderly performance and become a measurement of it.
3. **Add the rotation-normalised stream for ADL only**, with S4b guarding the fall head.
4. Then Charades becomes the *transfer* corpus rather than the primary, which also gives you a real cross-dataset protocol for Agent 2 — something P2 currently only has for falls.

## The redesign, and what it buys

I wrote the ingestion layer and measured the map against the real annotations. [toyota.py](src/behaviorsense/data/toyota.py), [audit_toyota_map.py](scripts/audit_toyota_map.py), 12 tests in [test_toyota.py](tests/test_toyota.py).

**Toyota replaces Charades for the ADL half.** 18 subjects aged 60–80, seven fixed cameras in one apartment — the population and the CCTV geometry we actually target, versus crowdworkers acting to a handheld camera. `Take_pills` alone gives 383 instances / 60,229 frames of real supervision for the class Charades reached through a single keyword rule.

**Train on the 51 fine classes, pool to coarse afterwards.** Collapsing before the loss destroys the supervision that separates members — all five `Cook.*` become one target, so the head is asked for one answer across cutting, stirring, stove and oven with no signal they differ. `collapse_matrix()` pools *after*, via logsumexp over members, so one checkpoint reports both the 51-class benchmark and the taxonomy Agent 3 consumes.

**Two coarse classes appended, ids 20–21.** `Use_laptop` (6.7% of frames), `Use_tablet` (5.2%), `Use_Drawer`, `Use_cupboard`, `Use_fridge`, `Put_/Take_something_on_table` — 18% of the corpus — would all have landed in `other_idle` under the obvious map. That is the Charades fallback mistake again. So `using_device` and `object_interaction` exist, each with a real `behaviour_role`. Measured result: **`other_idle` receives zero frames from Toyota**, versus Charades where the fallback was the largest class.

Appended, not renumbered, and that's the load-bearing detail: the shards store only the coarse label id, so re-partitioning 0–19 would cost the ~6 h re-extraction. Appending leaves every existing shard readable. `activity.py` deliberately stays at 20 classes until a 22-wide checkpoint exists, so today's demo keeps working — test T8 stops the two lists drifting.

**What Toyota cannot fix, stated plainly.** It supervises 15 of 22 coarse classes. Missing: `standing` and `sitting` (annotated only as the `Get_up`/`Sit_down` transitions — the sustained posture is unlabelled), `bending_reaching`, `falling`/`fallen_on_ground` (ADL corpus, no falls at all), `interacting_with_person` (one resident per recording), `other_idle`. A third of frames on average are unannotated gaps — and a gap most likely *contains* sitting or standing, so treating gaps as negatives would teach the model that sitting is absent. `frame_mask()` exists for exactly that: the 51-class benchmark head treats gaps as true negatives (correct there, and required for comparability), the cross-corpus head masks them. This makes the architecture a **partial-label multi-task** model — each corpus supervises what it defines and abstains on the rest. That's the honest version of "use every dataset".

Two deliberate deviations from what you asked:

- **I wrote an audit script, not a map generator.** For Charades a keyword-rule generator was justified by 157 names; its fallback is a large part of why we're at 0.128. All 82 Toyota names are mapped explicitly and `collapse_matrix()` *refuses* an unmapped class. Adding a rule engine would reintroduce the exact failure mode we're escaping.
- **Depth cannot be a model input**, because serving takes ordinary RGB from a phone or CCTV. Training on depth would create an input we can't supply. It's genuinely useful for privileged-information distillation (train with depth, infer without) — but that's a multi-week build. I'd use it now for occlusion/quality labels and pose QA, and revisit distillation only if the schedule holds. Same for the V1.2 skeletons: I'd extract COCO-17 with **our own RTMO** so training matches serving exactly, and use V1.2 as a pose-agreement QA signal and a candidate second stream. Training on 13-joint 3D LCRNet and serving 17-joint 2D RTMO is a guaranteed train/serve skew, and this project has already paid for that class of bug twice.

## What the trimmed loaders actually contain

**The two official repos number the same 31 classes differently.** This is the most dangerous thing in the corpus:

| repo | `Cook.Cleandishes` | `WatchTV` | id 0 means |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2s-AGCN-For-Daily-Living` (skeleton) | 0 | 30 | a real class |
| `i3d_smarthome` (RGB) | 1 | 31 | **"no name matched"** |

Both are official, both linked from the project page. `_name_to_int` initialises `integer=0` and falls through an if/elif chain, so an unrecognised filename silently becomes class 0 instead of raising. Read an RGB label file with the skeleton map and every class shifts by one, with a catch-all bucket underneath — no crash, no visible symptom, a plausible accuracy measuring nothing. `tsm_id(name, space="rgb"|"skeleton")` now forces the choice at the call site and `tsm_name(0, space="rgb")` refuses.

**Trimmed is 30 fps, untrimmed is 25.** The i3d repo decodes trimmed at 30; the TSU README mandates 25 because untrimmed ships at ×1.25 speed. Same apartment, same cameras, two frame rates. **The skeleton repo validates on the test set.** Its `gendata` has `part='val'` → `not istraining`, which for cross-subject *is* the test split. ## Qwen3.5-9B: better model, wrong fit

It's real — released February 2026, Apache-2.0, 9B dense, hybrid Gated DeltaNet + full attention, 262K context, and the reported benchmarks are genuinely strong for the size. Four problems, in order of severity:

**It doesn't fit the serving GPU.** 9B at 16-bit is ~18 GB of weights before any KV cache. A T4 gives ~15 GB usable, P100 gives 16. It only runs sharded across T4×2, and cross-device generation over PCIe is slow. Quantising to fit is the thing we explicitly refused — it would trade the numbers in `results/evaluation.md` for ones nobody has measured.

**The DeltaNet path needs `causal_conv1d` and `fla`, and without them [transformers' own docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/qwen3_5) say it "silently falls back to slower and more memory-hungry" paths.** Silent, memory-hungry, on a 16 GB card, is the precise failure class this project keeps paying for. Both are CUDA extensions that must match the Kaggle image, and notebook 04 is offline — so they'd have to be prebuilt wheels staged into `behaviorsense-wheels`.

**It wants `transformers >= 5.2`** ([NVIDIA's docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/nightly/models/qwen/qwen35-vl.html)) — a major version bump under `outlines>=1.0`, which is what provides the grammar-constrained decoding. That's an integration risk with a one-month deadline and a 2-hour feedback loop.

**All Qwen3.5 variants are natively multimodal.** That weakens your own architectural claim from structural to procedural: today "the LLM never sees pixels" is true because the model *cannot*; with a VLM it's true because *we don't send them*. The API surface still enforces it — no endpoint accepts images — but a text-only Agent 4 is the version an examiner can't poke a hole in.

**And the gain is on the wrong axis.** Hallucination sits at ~8%, stable across four reproduced runs, and grammar constraints didn't move it (p=0.79). The verifier catches unfaithful claims regardless of who wrote them — that's the contribution, and it's model-agnostic. What a stronger model buys is *yield*: fewer withheld claims, fewer truncations, fewer schema rejections. Real, but secondary.

### What I'd do instead

1. **Keep Qwen2.5-7B as the measured baseline.** Four reproduced runs a month from a deadline is a result, not a placeholder.
2. **If you want the upgrade, try Qwen3.5-4B, not 9B.** ~8 GB at 16-bit — fits a single T4 with headroom, same architecture family, and the reported small-model results are the strongest part of that release. Same harness, cheap ablation.
3. **For the live demo, route Agent 4 through the AgentRouter API.** Notebook 05 has internet ON. That frees all 16 GB for perception and activity, removes the model-size ceiling entirely, and the verifier is exactly what makes an untrusted remote author safe — C1–C4 check arithmetic regardless of who wrote the sentence. Live claims already go through `escapeHtml` before they reach the DOM.

   Keep local Qwen for notebook 04's numbers though. A hosted model changes under you, and a hallucination rate measured against a moving target isn't reproducible.

Three models behind one verifier is a better dissertation result than one bigger model — it demonstrates the guarantee is a property of the architecture, not of the checkpoint.

C5 reads every numeric literal in the claim text and checks at least one of them matches `claimed_value` within the same 2% relative tolerance C2 uses. ## What went wrong, and what I changed

**The parse error was two documented merges I hadn't implemented.** Your log gave me the schema — `event,start_frame,end_frame` with class *names* — and then died on `Make_coffee.Get_water`. That name isn't in the 51-class `Action_list` because the CSVs ship the **pre-merge 53-name vocabulary**. The dataset README says so:

> merge `Make_coffee.Get_water` & `Get Water` and `Insert_tea_bag` & `Make_tea.Insert_tea_bag` to have 51 action classes

I'd read that line and not acted on it. `TSU_ALIASES` now applies both merges, and every alias target is asserted to be a real class.

**The worse bug was the failure mode.** It examined *one file of 536*, raised, and told you nothing about `Make_tea.Insert_tea_bag` — which was in the same file, four lines later. Ninety-three minutes to learn one of two names. `survey_annotation_csvs()` now walks all 536 first and reports **every** unrecognised name with the file it appeared in, before any real parsing. A second surprise costs one run, not one run per name.

**78 of those 93 minutes were glob.** Nine `**` patterns over ~130,000 mounted files, each descending into `mp4/` (16,115) and `bounding_box_train/` (65,242). Replaced with bounded-depth resolution: datasets mount at `datasets/<owner>/<slug>/`, so each asset is a `(subdir, filename_glob)` pair tested with `is_dir()` and counted with `os.scandir`. `RESOLVE_CODE` got the same treatment — that cell alone was 15 minutes. Expect seconds now.

**`behaviorsense-code` contains MSMT17.** Your log shows the msmt17 pattern resolving inside the code mount — 65,242 restricted person crops, uploaded when the dataset was first created with `kaggle datasets create -p .` (the trap `docs/07` documents: `.kaggleignore` isn't read by the Kaggle CLI). `publish_code_dataset.py` now warns about restricted corpora in the working tree and **refuses** if one reaches the staged copy. ## The principle: serving parity

The deployment input is fixed: **arbitrary user-uploaded RGB → RTMO → 17-joint COCO 2D**. A phone video or CCTV feed has no Kinect. So anything that must exist at *serving* time can only be built from RGB. That kills depth and 3D skeletons as **direct model inputs** — not because they're low-quality (V1.2 is the opposite), but because a model that consumes them is a model you can never run for a user.

This isn't hypothetical caution. This project has already paid twice for train/serve skew: `normalise()` erased falls (AUROC 0.466), and the fall head's val AUROC 1.000 sat next to held-out 0.47 because in-domain negatives were separable by nuisance cues. Adding a third instance of that class of bug is the risk.

But "can't be an input" ≠ "can't help." Here's what each mount is actually for:

| mount | as direct input | legitimate train-time use |
|---|---|---|
| `toyota-smarthome-skeleton-v1-2` (16,115) | ✗ 15-joint 3D LCR-Net, serving is 17-joint 2D RTMO | **QA reference** + **extra occlusion-robust training windows** |
| `toyota-smarthome-skeleton` (V1.1) | ✗ | nothing — **superseded by V1.2** (SSTA-PRS refined it for exactly occlusion/truncation). Using both invites citing the wrong version |
| `pose-untrimmed` (536) | ✗ | same as V1.2, untrimmed half — only relevant if the untrimmed extraction proves its worth |
| `toyota-smarthome-depth` (both) | ✗ no depth at serving | **distillation teacher only** (train with depth, infer without) |
| `msmt17` | ✗ | already used — the ReID operating point τ=0.355 is *fitted on it* |

## The three real uses, ranked by gain-per-day

**1. V1.2 as a QA reference for the extraction — cheap, do it first (~2–3 h).**
SSTA-PRS refined these skeletons specifically to fix occlusion and truncation — which is precisely RTMO's weakness. Sampling ~100 clips and comparing RTMO's per-joint visibility against V1.2's gives you a *measured* answer to "how often does our pose estimator fail, and on which activities" — the exact failure mode that produces confident nonsense windows. That number also belongs in the dissertation as a perception-quality result.

**2. V1.2 converted to COCO-17 windows as extra training data — real lever, decide after the first Toyota numbers (~1 day).**
The conversion is mechanical: project 3D→2D (orthographic + bbox scaling; our `normalise()` makes windows scale/translation invariant, so pixel-exactness matters less than it seems), map 15→17 joints, set the 5 missing face joints to confidence 0. That yields occlusion-robust windows for exactly the classes that are starving — `personal_hygiene` at 9,360 frames and `taking_medication` at 0.56% are the ones where extra windows could actually move F1. The risk is estimator-domain gap (LCR-Net 2D ≠ RTMO 2D distribution), which is why I'd **measure first**: if the plain RTMO-trained 31-class head lands near the published ceiling already, the marginal gain is small and this stays cut; if the tail classes are starving, this is the cheapest fix available.

**3. Depth via privileged distillation — the big one, and the one to cut (~2 days + retraining).**
Train a teacher on depth+3D (where occlusion doesn't exist), distill its logits into the RTMO student. Literature gain is 1–3 points and it's the only way depth contributes at serving. But it's a second model family, a distillation harness, and a retraining cycle — with one month left, Toyota base training and RT-DETR wiring both outrank it.

- **With 07's output in hand:** I add the V1.2 QA comparison (use 1) — it's a small standalone step, and it needs the extraction's RTMO output to compare against anyway.
- **Decision point:** use 2 goes in only if the first Toyota training shows starving tail classes. Use 3 stays cut unless everything else lands early.

The meta-point: "not used as input" was never "not used." V1.2 and depth are mounted and licensed; the question is only which of the three train-time roles earns its integration cost before your deadline. If the first extraction histogram shows starvation, use 2 jumps the queue.

- **Pre-merge 53-name vocabulary** vs post-merge 51-class `Action_list`.
- **Frame-level vs span-set annotation agreement** — a pure span split scores 1.00000 at frame level.
- **Fine-then-pool** — train on 51/31 fine classes, derive coarse via logsumexp over `collapse_matrix()` members. Collapsing before the loss destroys discriminative supervision.
- **Partial-label masked loss** — each corpus supervises the classes it defines and abstains on the rest.
- **C1–C5 verifier**: C1 ref_exists, C2 value_matches, C3 pct_matches, C4 direction_consistent, **C5 prose_quoted_value** (new).
- **Privileged-information distillation** — train with depth/3D, infer without.
- **Serving parity** — deployment input is fixed as RGB → RTMO → 17-joint COCO 2D.
- Grammar-constrained decoding via `outlines`; `force_greedy()`; two hallucination denominators (schema-valid vs emitted).

## 5. Problem Solving

**Toyota Smarthome research** — identified the proven pipelines: untrimmed = `dairui01/Toyota_Smarthome` (I3D features + PDAN, **32.7% f-mAP CS**) and `dairui01/MS-TCT`; trimmed skeleton = `YangDi666/2s-AGCN-For-Daily-Living`; trimmed RGB = `srijandas07/i3d_smarthome` (which ships `models/rgb_SH_CS.pt`, I3D trained on Smarthome CS with **SSD person crops** — the same input shape our RTMO boxes produce).

**The redesign** — retarget Agent 2 from Charades (actor-disjoint macro-F1 0.128) to Toyota (18 subjects aged 60–80, seven fixed cameras, real ADL taxonomy including `Take_pills`). Train fine, pool coarse. Append taxonomy ids 20–21 rather than renumbering (shards store only the coarse id, so re-partitioning 0–19 would need the ~6 h re-extraction). Toyota supervises 15 of 22 coarse classes; the other 7 must be masked.

**Modality decisions** (answering "why not the other datasets") — serving parity is the principle: deployment is RGB → RTMO → 17-joint COCO 2D, so depth and 15-joint 3D skeletons can't be direct inputs. Three legitimate train-time roles ranked: V1.2 as QA reference (~2–3 h, do first); V1.2→COCO-17 as extra occlusion-robust windows (~1 day, gated on whether the first Toyota training shows starving tail classes); depth via privileged distillation (~2 days, cut for now). V1.1 is superseded by V1.2.

**Qwen3.5-9B analysis** — exists (Feb 2026, Apache-2.0, hybrid Gated DeltaNet, 262K context, natively multimodal), but: 18 GB weights don't fit one 16 GB serving card; DeltaNet needs `causal_conv1d`/`fla` or it "silently falls back to slower and more memory-hungry" paths; needs `transformers>=5.2` under `outlines>=1.0`; multimodality weakens the pixel-boundary claim from structural to procedural; and the gain is on the wrong axis (verifier catches unfaithful claims regardless). Recommended keeping 2.5-7B as the measured baseline, trying 3.5-4B as an ablation, and routing Agent 4 through AgentRouter for the live demo.

## The problem

**6,040 of 16,115 clips (37.5%) unusable** — and the loss was not uniform:

| coarse class | windows | share | annotated corpus share |

| `sitting_down` | **233** | 0.24% | 0.72% |

Three to four times under-represented. The cause is arithmetic: at 20 fps source and `FPS_SAMPLE = 12.5`, the integer stride is `round(20/12.5) = 2` → effective **10 Hz** → a 30-frame window spans **3.0 s** → any clip shorter than 3 s yields *no window at all*. A sit-to-stand **is** a short clip. Your preflight even showed one: `Sitdown_p20_r07_v09_c01.mp4`, 53 frames = 2.65 s.

Those two classes are what Agent 3 derives `sit_to_stand_count` from — a validated clinical frailty marker. That's a headline feature being starved, not a tail statistic. And 149 windows is the same range as Charades' `standing` (123 → F1 0.005) and `bending_reaching` (26 → 0.000).

## Fixed

- **`FPS_SAMPLE = 20.0`** → stride 1, window **1.50 s**, minimum clip 1.5 s. Estimated **~322k windows** vs 97,787. And 1.50 s is *closer* to the Charades shards' 2.0 s than 3.00 s was, so window-extent consistency improves at the same time.
- **Adaptive stride**: a clip too short for the nominal stride now gets a *finer* rate rather than being discarded. Thirty timesteps over less real time is a speed perturbation — a standard augmentation, and strictly better than having no example of the activity.
- **Named drop reasons + stride histogram**, in the log and the manifest. The first run said "6,040 unusable" and nothing about why; finding the cause needed arithmetic on the class histogram afterwards.
- **The rate is now in the shard name** (`toyota_trimmed_20hz_0000.npz`), so re-running at a different rate can't resume against shards whose windows span a different duration and mix two rates into one training set.

The transitions recovered 8–9×, which was the whole point — `sit_to_stand_count` is supportable now instead of resting on 149 windows. Smallest fine class is ~205 windows against `MIN_SUPPORT = 50`; for comparison Charades left `bending_reaching` at 26 and `standing` at 123.

**Toyota is now the larger corpus**: 214,913 windows against Charades' 165,109.

Two things the diagnostics confirm cleanly. `strides used: {1: 16115}` — no clip needed the adaptive path, so the nominal rate was already right. And all 909 remaining drops are **`no window passed the visibility gate`** — genuine pose failures from occlusion or truncation, *not* striding. That's the honest residual, and at 5.6% it's exactly the territory the V1.2 refined skeletons were built for (SSTA-PRS fixed occlusion/truncation). Much less compelling than 37.5% was, but it's the recoverable remainder if the tail classes need it.

My 322k window estimate was 50% high — actual 215k. The recovered clips are short and contribute 1–2 windows each, so windows/clip came out 14.1 rather than 20.

## One thing I fixed before you run the untrimmed half

Integer striding would have broken window-duration parity between the two halves: 20 fps trimmed → 20 Hz → 1.50 s, but 25 fps untrimmed → 25 Hz → **1.20 s**. Same 30-frame tensor, different real time, and no field recording which — the two shard sets wouldn't be comparable.

`poses_for` now does **exact resampling** (`want = int(round(k * src / rate))`) instead of integer striding. Verified by simulation: 20 fps keeps 1200/1200 frames, 25 fps keeps 1200/1500, and a 30-frame window spans **1.45 s vs 1.44 s** — parity. It's also capped at the container rate so it can never resample *up* and invent motion. The log now reports effective rates and `window_seconds` goes into the manifest.

## The hazard

Save Version publishes **whatever is in `/kaggle/working`**. The carry-forward loop only copied shards matching the *current* prefix — so an untrimmed run would have copied forward `toyota_untrimmed_20hz_*` (nothing, first run), extracted its own, and published a dataset version containing **only the untrimmed half**. Your 214,913 trimmed windows would have vanished from the latest version — recoverable from the old version, but you'd only discover it when training came up short.

Fixed: carry-forward now copies **every** `toyota_*.npz`, while `DONE` still keys on the current prefix so a rate or mode change re-extracts rather than assuming another shard set's clips are done. The verify cell now prints what the Save Version will actually publish:

```
the dataset this Save Version will publish:
  toyota_trimmed_20hz            214,913 windows
  toyota_untrimmed_20hz           NN,NNN windows
  TOTAL                          NNN,NNN windows in NN shard(s)
```

N23 pins it, with a negative control confirming the prefix-only version fails. `181/181`.

## What landed

**[multicorpus.py](src/behaviorsense/data/multicorpus.py)** — the piece that makes training on 365k Toyota windows *alongside* Charades safe rather than actively harmful.

The problem it solves: Toyota covers 15 of 22 coarse classes and structurally cannot cover the rest. It annotates `Sit_down` as a transition and never labels the sustained posture; a third of its frames are unannotated gaps where sitting is most likely. Under plain cross-entropy, every one of those 365,492 windows becomes a statement that the resident is **not** sitting — training the model to suppress exactly the classes Charades is there to teach.

`masked_cross_entropy` masks unsupervisable classes to `-inf` **before** the softmax. That distinction is the whole thing, and it's the tempting wrong implementation to get backwards: zeroing a masked class's loss *afterwards* leaves it in the normaliser, so predicting it is still penalised and the model still learns "Toyota windows aren't sitting."

Measured, in M1:

```
gradient on `sitting`, Toyota row:   0.000000   ← exactly zero, all 9 unsupervised classes
gradient on `sitting`, Charades row: -0.472222   ← still supervised
```

Also in place:

- **`CorpusSpec` per shard tag.** An unknown tag **raises** rather than defaulting to "supervise everything" — that default would silently reintroduce the bug for whichever corpus was added last. Toyota's supervised sets are *derived* from the maps, so adding a class can't leave the mask behind.

I can't confirm from a screenshot which one you hit, so I fixed both and made the residue visible.

**A pose can exist and be entirely below threshold.** `kp` is non-null, so the dashed "pose unusable" branch is skipped — then every edge and joint is skipped by `MIN_SCORE = 0.3`, and it renders *literally nothing*. A person in plain view becomes empty space while a weaker detection elsewhere gets a full skeleton. Absent and unusable were meant to look different; this was an invisible third state. **The scale factor divided by the container's claim, not the decoded frame.** Keypoints are in `frame.shape` space; `width`/`height` came from `CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH/HEIGHT`, which disagrees on any file with a rotation matrix, non-square pixels, or a wrong header. ## The classifier was fed 3-second windows. It has only ever seen 2-second ones.

Your clip is 20 fps. Serving computed `out_fps = src_fps / 2` → **10 Hz**, and a 30-frame window at 10 Hz is **3.0 s of motion**. The ADL shards were built at `FPS_SAMPLE = 15`, so ST-GCN++ has never seen a window longer than 2.0 s. Every action in your video arrived **stretched 1.5×**.

`out_fps = src_fps / 2` is correct on exactly one input: a 30 fps source. 20 fps → 10 Hz. 25 fps → 12.5 Hz.

This is the same defect notebook 07 already cost you a 12,796 s GPU run for — it strided with `round(src / nominal)`, every trimmed clip was 20 fps, a nominal 12.5 Hz became an effective 10 Hz, and 37.5% of clips came out unusable. The fix there was exact resampling; the serving path never received it. Now it does, with notebook 07's own formula:

```
20 fps → 15.0 Hz → 2.00 s   ✓
25 fps → 15.0 Hz → 2.00 s   ✓
30 fps → 15.0 Hz → 2.00 s   ✓
10 fps → 10.0 Hz → 3.00 s   declared, not faked
```

A sub-15 fps camera can't reach the rate, so Agent 1 now says so rather than absorbing it as bad accuracy — verified rendering: *"Its 3.00 s windows carry 1.50× the motion of the 2.0 s windows ST-GCN++ has seen, so Agent 2's labels are outside the conditions any measured number covers."*

I can't promise this alone fixes the labels. It removes a distortion that was guaranteed to be hurting them.

## My regression, and it was the worst possible one

`overlay.sizeDisagreement is not a function` — your browser had the old `overlay.js` cached. But the real fault is mine: I called it **before** `renderStages`, so a missing *diagnostic* threw and the C1–C5 table never rendered. A warning suppressed the entire point of the page. The render now goes first, and the call is `typeof`-guarded — a stale module costs you a diagnostic, never the results.

Sampling doesn't explain everything. `interacting_with_person` is the **second-worst class in the measured table** — [results/evaluation.md:207](results/evaluation.md:207): F1 **0.042**, precision 0.036 on 614 windows. `cleaning_housework` is 0.098, and `cooking_food_prep` — what she was actually doing — is 0.187 on only 419 training windows. Your output is close to what those numbers predict.

Advising someone to "reach out for assistance" off 30 seconds is wrong regardless of the labels, and the reliability flag is computed and then ignored by the reporter. INRIA's Toyota skeleton benchmark is **2s-AGCN on their released 3D poses**, and their loader (`read_xyz`) takes LCR-Net's 13 joints and derives two midpoints — neck from the shoulders, mid-hip from the hips — giving the 15 nodes their published graph is indexed against. ## The reader sniffs, because their format isn't documented

No README specifies `*_pose3d.json`. This project has paid for trusting an unspecified format once — notebook 06 spent 93 minutes before dying on `Make_coffee.Get_water`. So `read_pose3d` handles the plausible layouts and *reports* what it found when it can't. Verified against five: bare list, `frames` key, transposed `[3,J]`, flat 39-vector, and a dict keyed by frame index.

Two behaviours are load-bearing beyond parsing:

- **An empty frame survives as missing, zero-filled, `present=False`.** LCR-Net finding nobody is a fact. Dropping the frame shortens the clip and desynchronises every frame-indexed annotation — the alignment `frame_multilabel` exists to hold.
- **A frame-index dict sorts numerically.** String order puts `"10"` before `"2"` and shuffles the clip into nonsense that still has the right shape.

It also reports coordinate ranges, which is the cheapest way to tell metres from pixels from normalised units — all three occur in released pose data, and each needs different normalisation.

## The dangerous part: `pose3d` is 39 flat floats

39 = 13 × 3, and **both** readings reshape without error:

```
[x0..x12, y0..y12, z0..z12]     coordinate-major  ← builds a body
[x0,y0,z0, x1,y1,z1, ...]       joint-major       ← swaps joints for coordinates
```

The wrong one trains perfectly well on nonsense and is invisible in a loss curve. My earlier speculative reader did `reshape(13, 3)` — **joint-major**. That was wrong and would have scrambled every skeleton.

LCR-Net's own visualiser is the authority: it plots joint `i` at `(pose2d[i], pose2d[i + njts])`, so y sits `njts` positions later — coordinate-major. But I'm not shipping that on my memory of their code. `verify_lcrnet_layout()` re-derives it from the data anatomically: ankles below knees below hips below shoulders below head in image y, scored over every frame. A joint-major file scores near zero on that chain.

`read_pose3d()` runs the check on load and **refuses** a file whose layout contradicts the constant, naming both scores. The negative control confirms it — a correctly-built body written joint-major is rejected, not read.

## Two other things the numbers tell us

**2D poses can fall outside the frame.** `Cook.Usestove_p11` reaches x=747 on a 640-wide frame; `P09T14C07` reaches x=−61.7 and y=705.5. That's normal for LCR-Net — it regresses full-body poses from anchors, so occluded limbs get extrapolated past the image edge. Harmless for the 2s-AGCN path, which uses 3D, but any consumer of `pose2d` must not assume bounds. Worth knowing if you ever use these as a QA reference against RTMO.

**The 3D is root-relative, not camera-absolute.** Every file spans roughly ±0.5–1.5 m with a third coordinate that goes negative — a human body near an origin, not a person 2–4 m from a lens. That's good for ADL recognition, and it confirms with evidence something I'd only argued before: root-relative coordinates discard global motion, which is exactly what made `normalise()` drive fall AUROC to 0.466. **Falls cannot come from this representation later** — they'll need the RTMO 2D path, where absolute image position survives. ## The "MIXED" layout is my scorer failing, not the archives disagreeing

11 files of 1,736 scored `joint_major`: 6 in V1.1, 6 in V1.2, 5 in untrimmed. Two things say those are artefacts, not a mixed format:

**The counts match across releases.** V1.1 and V1.2 are independently produced — V1.2 was re-refined by SSTA-PRS — so a genuine *format* split would not land on 6 files in both. A *clip*-dependent cause would.

**My scorer is anatomy-based, and anatomy fails on non-upright subjects.** `upright_chain_score` requires ankles below knees below hips below shoulders below head. Seated or lying, that chain is legitimately meaningless — `WatchTV_p02` scored 0.007, `Drink.Fromcup_p20` 0.09, and `Laydown_*` appears in the drop list. When both hypotheses score near zero, noise picks the winner, and my code called that a verdict.

I compute the margin already and then threw it away in the verdict. A truly wrong layout scores ~1.0 vs ~0.0 (margin 1.0, as in the synthetic test); a posture artefact scores ~0.02 vs ~0.01. Those are not the same finding and shouldn't read the same.

**This was about to break the training run.** `read_pose3d` defaults to `verify_layout=True` and *raises* on disagreement — so the pipeline would have crashed on ~1% of the corpus, on files that are fine. Now a disagreement only counts when the joint-major reading genuinely looks like an upright human (score ≥ 0.5 **and** margin ≥ 0.2), which cannot happen by accident. Below that it's recorded as inconclusive and the file is read with the assumed layout.

## The graph network accepts 15 joints

`build_adjacency` was hard-wired to COCO-17 — module-scope `N_JOINTS`, `COCO_EDGES`, `centre = 0`. Now parameterised, COCO defaults byte-identical. Toyota's graph centres on the **pelvis**, which is anatomically what Yan et al.'s three-partition strategy wants; COCO-17 uses the nose only because it has no spine joint.

Added an orphan check: a joint disconnected from the centre has infinite hop distance, lands in no partition, and receives no messages — it trains as a constant, invisibly. `STGCNpp(n_classes=31, n_joints=15, adjacency=A, n_person=1)` forwards to 786,955 params.

`to_bone` now takes an explicit parent map. Its `max(i, j)` heuristic only identifies the child when edges happen to be listed root-outward; Toyota's tree states direction outright. Verified the torch and numpy derivations agree exactly.

## But the remaining 73 are my heuristic being fooled, not a mixed archive

Same class profile as before — five of the eight shown are `Drink.From*`, plus `Cook.Cleanup` and `Cutbread`, and `Drink.Fromcup_p19_r03_v03_c05` / `_v04_c05` are adjacent takes of one subject. A genuine format split would scatter across classes and cameras; this clusters by posture and viewpoint exactly as the first batch did.

There's a mechanism. Reading coordinate-major 2D as joint-major gives "joint 0..5" from x-values only and "joint 7..12" from y-values only. The upright chain then satisfies *hips > shoulders > head* structurally, and the ankle/knee links reduce to coin flips on millimetre x-differences. So a roughly symmetric body can score high under the wrong reading by construction. My discriminator can't tell those apart, and I shouldn't reject files on it.

**The right fix is to stop rejecting per file.** The layout question is archive-wide — a transposition is a property of how the release was written, not of one clip. That question is already answered decisively: coordinate-major, unanimous across 1,725 files where anatomy speaks, and confirmed by LCR-Net's own visualiser. So:

- the corpus-level check runs **once** at the start of a build over a sample, and aborts everything if the decisive files disagree
- every file is then read with the confirmed constant, per-file scores recorded for audit, **never rejected**

## What it reports and why both numbers

Top-1 **and** mean per-class, always. On an 88× imbalance they answer different questions — top-1 is dominated by `Walk`'s 3,942 clips, mean per-class is what the Toyota paper reports precisely so the tail can't be ignored. Publishing one would be a silent choice about which classes matter.

The checkpoint is selected on **mean per-class**, not top-1, for the same reason: top-1 would pick the epoch that best fits the majority class.

Class weighting is effective-number (Cui et al.), not inverse frequency — 1/n would weight `Cutbread`'s 45 clips 88× a `Walk` clip, which assumes each tail sample carries 88× the information. Tail clips of one action by one subject overlap heavily; they don't.

Every per-class accuracy prints its **test support and its own granularity**. `Cutbread` will have roughly 15 test clips, so its accuracy moves in steps of ~7 points — that belongs beside the value, not discovered when someone quotes it.

## Two guards that will fire if something's wrong

The script asserts no subject crosses the CS boundary, independently of the shard builder — Charades leaked actors for months and cost macro-F1 0.152 → 0.128 when fixed. ## My logsumexp prediction was wrong, by −0.145

I argued pooling siblings' logits before deciding must beat collapsing the argmax. It's worse: 0.5910 against 0.7363. The mechanism is visible in the per-class column:

```
cooking_food_prep   0.934    11 fine members
walking             0.151     3 fine members
reading             0.348     1
```

`walking` has the *most* test clips (1,333) and its fine members score 0.760 / 0.936 / 0.925 individually — so argmax-collapse puts it near 0.79. Pooling crushed it to 0.151, and `cooking_food_prep` absorbed the predictions.

**LogSumExp over k comparable terms is ≈ max + log(k).** An 11-member class therefore gets an unearned +log(11) ≈ +2.4 over a single-member class. Mathematically, summing probabilities *is* correct marginalisation — but only over a calibrated posterior. This model is trained with label smoothing 0.1 and class-balanced weights, so it spreads diffuse mass across all eleven cooking classes on nearly every input, and `cooking_food_prep` wins by accumulation rather than evidence.

So the honest statement is narrower than my claim: marginalising an **uncalibrated** posterior over unequal family sizes systematically favours large families. That's a testable defect, not a dead end — temperature calibration before pooling is exactly what the dumped logits let us check for nothing.

## Final configuration: no post-hoc knobs at all

```
bone stream, tau = 0, T = 1, argmax collapse
fine   (31 classes)          top-1 0.6779   mean per-class 0.5935
coarse (13 of 22 classes)    top-1 0.7694   mean per-class 0.7363
```

**τ is worthless here.** τ=0.25 buys +0.0011 fine mean-class — noise — and costs 0.058 top-1. Every larger τ is monotonically worse, and on coarse it's strictly harmful: 0.7363 → 0.7173 → 0.6530 → 0.5959 → 0.5087.

On Charades this was the *strongest* lever, +0.053 mean-class. I expected the same by analogy and the analogy failed. The reason is concrete: this run already carries effective-number loss weights (β=0.9999) plus label smoothing, so the tail was up-weighted **during** training. Applying a prior correction on top double-corrects. Charades needed τ because its residual imbalance was uncorrected. Same mechanism, opposite conclusion — which is why it got measured instead of assumed.

**Pooling never wins.** As T falls to 0.25 logsumexp converges up toward argmax (0.7340 vs 0.7363) and never crosses. My synthetic test showed a crossing was *possible*; on the real logits it doesn't happen. So the `log(k)` family-size advantage is not a calibration artefact — it's real, and argmax collapse is correct. Closed.

The upside of all this: the quotable configuration has **no tuned post-hoc parameters**. Nothing to justify, nothing to explain away as fitted on the test split.

## Does checkpointing cost accuracy? No — but I found the trap it hides

`torch.save`/`load_state_dict` is bit-exact, so the round-trip loses nothing. Two things are worth knowing:

**`best.pt` is strictly better than `last.pt` here** — 0.6000 at ep13 versus 0.5932 at ep21. Early stopping saved you from the worse model.

**The real trap: `best.pt` holds two sets of weights.** `train_adl.py` saves `"model": model.state_dict()` *and* `"ema": ema.shadow` — and 0.6000 was measured on the **EMA** weights (`ema.copy_to(eval_model)`), not on `"model"`. Loading `ck["model"]` would give you a model that has never been evaluated and would score lower.

I checked whether serving gets this right, and it does: `EnsembleClassifier` defaults `use_ema=True` and prefers `ck["ema"]`. So the answer is no accuracy loss — but only because that default exists. ## Will checkpointing reduce accuracy?

**No — but there was a real trap, and it's already guarded.**

`train_adl.py` evaluates the **EMA** weights (`ema.copy_to(eval_model)`) but saves `{"model": raw_state_dict, "ema": ema.shadow}` — two different sets of weights in one file. Your 0.6000 describes the EMA ones. Loading `ck["model"]` would give you a *different, worse* model while looking correct.

`EnsembleClassifier` already handles it: `use_ema=True` by default and `state = ck.get("ema") if ... else ck.get("model", ck)`. So serving loads exactly what was measured. Save/load itself is bit-exact — same dtype, no quantisation.

## What the wiring does

**The checkpoint is resolved by content, not by directory name.** Your run wrote `adl_toyota_bone/`; the Charades run wrote `adl_bone/`. A name-built path finds neither when both are attached. Every checkpoint records its own `args.stream`, `args.n_classes` and the shard paths it trained on, so the notebook reads those and prints every candidate with its metrics before choosing.

`ADL_PREFER = "toyota"` picks between them and the alternatives are printed, because with both datasets mounted that choice is real and silently serving the Charades model would look completely normal.

**The sample rate is derived from the checkpoint's own shard paths**, not from a constant. It greps `_20hz_` out of `args.shards` and sets `STATE["sample_fps"] = 20.0`, which `/video` then passes to the decode child. Serving Toyota weights at 15 Hz would stretch every action 1.33× — the same defect as the old `src_fps / 2` stride wearing a different hat. Deriving it from the shards makes the pair impossible to separate.

## Toyota's demo is not the same task

The demos they publish are **RGB** models — I3D, VPN, PDAN — running on **Toyota's own test split**: same apartment, same seven fixed cameras, same recording conditions as training. Published *skeleton-only* results on that benchmark sit around 0.5–0.6 mean per-class, not near-perfect. Yours measured 0.60.

So the pipeline is roughly where skeleton-only methods land. That does not make this output acceptable — a 30-second cooking clip labelled `taking_medication` is wrong by any standard — but "their model got everything right" is comparing an RGB model on in-distribution footage against a skeleton model on a random internet video. Different task.

## The likely cause is `Temperature 1.00`

Your log says it, and my own notebook comment predicted it: an unfitted temperature means "Viterbi and abstention consume meaningless posteriors."

The chain: the Toyota run dumped **no val logits**, so no temperature could be fitted → T=1.0 → `self_transition = 0.9` in Viterbi → **28 windows collapsed into 1 segment**. Whatever class had the highest average score won all 30 seconds. That's why you got one label instead of a timeline.

Worth noting how strong that wrong signal was: `fuse_objects` applies `MEDICATION_ABSENT_PENALTY = -2.0` to `taking_medication` when no pill bottle is detected, and no objects are detected at all. So class 12 was penalised by −2.0 log-odds and *still* won.

`train_adl.py` now dumps `val_logits.npz` at the selected epoch. One more training run makes calibration possible.

## But I can't prove that yet, so I added the diagnostic

A single segment spanning a whole clip is either a confident correct call or Viterbi collapsing uncalibrated windows — the segment list alone cannot distinguish them. `/video` now returns **`window_top3`**: the top-3 posteriors for each window Agent 2 saw.

If `cooking_food_prep` sits at 0.3 in second place across every window, that's calibration and Viterbi. If `taking_medication` is at 0.9 everywhere, the model genuinely believes it and the problem is training. Guessing between those is what I've been doing.

## Two other fixes from your report

**The rate banner was accusing the correct configuration.** It compared against `video.SHARD_FPS = 15.0` — a Charades constant — so your properly-served 20 Hz run was told its labels were outside measured conditions. It now compares against the rate actually being served.

**The overlay waiting for Qwen** is real: Agent 1 finished at 42.9 s, the overlay appeared at 330 s. The per-frame skeletons only travel in the final `result`, not in the Agent 1 stage event. That needs the frames moved into the stage — I haven't done it yet and it's next.

Found it. This is not a training problem — it's a train/serve skew, and it's the fourth of the same kind.

## The model is fed raw pixels at serving time. It was trained on torso-normalised units.

`SkeletonWindowDataset.__getitem__` calls `normalise(x)` — root-centres each person and divides by torso length, so training coordinates are **dimensionless, order ±2**.

`frames_to_windows` → `EnsembleClassifier.logits` on the serving path calls it **nowhere**. Every window reaching the model carries **raw 640×480 pixel coordinates, order ±300**.

That's roughly a 150× scale difference on every joint. The network is receiving inputs two orders of magnitude outside anything it has seen, so it saturates and returns one constant class — which is exactly your symptom:

- `Segments emitted 1`, identical `29.3s` across two runs — deterministic, input-independent
- `taking_medication` won **despite** `MEDICATION_ABSENT_PENALTY = −2.0`
- 28 windows collapsing to one state

I blamed the uncalibrated temperature last turn. Temperature scales logits; it cannot rescue inputs 150× out of range. That was the wrong diagnosis and this one is checkable rather than inferred.

## So: no, retraining on INRIA's exact pipeline would not have fixed this

I already built and ran their skeleton pipeline — 2s-AGCN's 15-joint graph, their CS split, their metrics. It scored 0.5935 fine / **0.7363 coarse**, which is where skeleton methods land on that benchmark. That model is sound.

Neither model can produce sensible output while serving feeds it pixels instead of torso units. Retraining anything before fixing this would have burned another session and returned the same 29.3 s segment, because the defect is downstream of every checkpoint.

It's also the same shape as the three we already fixed: `sys.path` not crossing a process boundary, integer striding instead of exact resampling, container size instead of decoded size. In each case one side of a pair was changed and the other wasn't.

## What I'm doing

`normalise()` goes onto the serving path, with an assertion that the coordinate scale a window carries is the scale the checkpoint was trained on — so this cannot recur silently. The one-line version isn't enough: `keep_root_motion` and the detection-dropout handling both matter, and `EnsembleClassifier` should refuse a window whose magnitude says it was never normalised, rather than returning a confident answer.

I also owe you a correction: `window_top3` went into the payload but I never rendered it, so the diagnostic I asked you to send was invisible on the page. That's why you pasted the same card twice. With normalisation fixed it should become unnecessary, but I'm wiring the display anyway — if the top-3 had been visible, this would have shown up as one class at ~1.0 across every window, which is saturation, not a close call.

The checkpoint scored 0.60 mean-class / 0.5854 macro-F1 on held-out Toyota subjects — a real number, measured through the *training* data path, which normalises. ## Fixed, and made non-repeatable

**`ActivityPipeline.run` now normalises**, matching what training does.

**`EnsembleClassifier.logits()` now refuses pixel-scale input.** This is the part that matters more than the fix. The convention was "the caller normalises", and of two callers exactly one honoured it — notebook 04's eval cell calls `normalise()` explicitly, which is how I knew the convention existed at all. A convention that two places must remember independently is a defect waiting for its third caller.

```
raw pixels refused: windows peak at 420 in x/y, which is pixel scale, not the torso units...
normalised peak 2.39 -> logits (4, 22)
```

The threshold is 25, and the reasoning is in the constant: normalised joints sit within ~2 torso lengths of the hip, plus a few more from retained root motion across a window — call it 10 at the extreme. A 640×480 frame peaks at 300–700. The gap between 10 and 300 is what makes 25 a line rather than a tuned value.

|---|---|---|---|
| T4 | 8.1 TFLOPS | 320 GB/s | no — model is fp32 |
| P100 | 9.3 TFLOPS | **732 GB/s** | n/a (Pascal has none) |

Pose extraction is bandwidth-heavy, and P100 has 2.3× the memory bandwidth. Your ~40 s for 601 frames should drop meaningfully. T4's tensor cores only mattered for Qwen — which is leaving.
