## So both, correctly

`torch_supports_device()` asks the wheel rather than the driver: compares `get_device_capability()` against `get_arch_list()`, and honours `compute_XX` PTX entries only where they can actually help — PTX lets a newer card run older code, never the reverse.

When PyTorch has no kernels:
- **ST-GCN++ runs on CPU.** 787k parameters over ~28 windows is a fraction of a second. That's the right answer, not a degradation.
- **OSNet runs on CPU too** — and this needed a real change. It lives in the decode child alongside RTMO, and the child took a single `device`. `extract_isolated` now takes a separate `osnet_device`, because "which device for the ONNX model" and "which device for the torch model" are different questions that happened to share a variable.
- **RTMO keeps the GPU.**

```

Capped at 3 now, and the array walks the chain *forward* from the current model rather than always leading with the primary, so a three-slot hint never re-offers something already tried, and a model that just returned `rate-limited upstream` doesn't keep a slot. The Python sweep still walks all five, so this truncates the routing hint, not the coverage.

My 400-handler assumed any 400 while constrained meant the model had refused the schema. So it **dropped server-side schema enforcement and re-sent the same malformed body** — trading away the one guarantee `constrained=True` buys, to work around something that had nothing to do with it. That's the kind of silent downgrade this architecture is specifically built to not do.

It now reads the body: schema markers → drop enforcement and retry once, recorded and declared in `name`; anything else → raise with the body verbatim, because a malformed request is malformed for every key and model. why is there a 60MB limit on uploads?

Because I picked the number, and unlike the frame cap next to it, it has no comment justifying it — `MAX_UPLOAD_MB = 60` at [_generate.py:3041](notebooks/_generate.py:3041) sits bare between two well-documented constants.

It also isn't the limit you're actually hitting. The binding one is:

```python
MAX_FRAMES = 900   # src/behaviorsense/video.py:54
```

At 20 Hz that's **45 seconds of video**, and it *refuses* rather than truncates — deliberately, per its own comment: "a report over the first 20 seconds of a ten-minute video, presented as a report over the video, is the kind of quiet misrepresentation this project keeps finding and removing." Your clip was 601 frames, so 30 s, comfortably under.

A 45-second 640×480 clip is a few megabytes. To reach 60 MB inside 900 frames you'd need something like 4K or near-lossless, where decode time would break first. So in every realistic case the size cap is inert.

What the size check *is* genuinely for — and this part I'd defend:

- It runs **before the streaming response begins**, while an HTTP status is still available. Once headers are sent for the NDJSON stream, 413 and 422 stop being options ([_generate.py:3673](notebooks/_generate.py:3673)).
- It's checked incrementally against 1 MiB chunks written straight to disk, so a huge body can't exhaust Kaggle's RAM before the check fires. That's also why the RAM ceiling isn't a function of this number.

So it's a coarse guard against someone posting a 2 GB file, not a considered capacity figure. 60 was a guess.

The real wart is the ordering. Size is checked as bytes arrive; frames are counted only after decode starts. So a 55 MB three-minute 1080p clip passes the size check, gets fully transferred and written to disk, and *then* gets rejected for frame count. And nothing tells you either limit up front — `/health` returns `max_upload_mb` but no part of the page renders it, and the file picker is a bare `accept="video/*"`.

If you want, the fix is small and worth doing: state the limit in the unit you experience it in — "clips up to 45 s" — on the upload control, and have the 413 name the duration cap as well as the byte cap. That's a copy change plus surfacing two fields the backend already sends.

`frameAt()` **clamped**. 900 frames at 20 Hz is exactly 45.0 s of analysis; your clips are 9:56 and 15:07. So from 45 s to the end, every redraw returned `frames[899]` — the last analysed pose, pinned. I ran the arithmetic: at t=149 s (the 2:29 in your first screenshot) the old code returns frame 899.

## 2. The person count — detection dropout, and the damage is worse than the count

From your own counters:

- **Video 1:** 623 person-records over 900 frames → no detection in ~31% of frames → 3 ids.
- **Video 2:** 456 records over 900 frames → no detection in ~49% → 9 ids minted (0,1,2,3,5,6,7,8 listed; id 4 produced nothing).

`max_age_frames = 30`, and its comment claimed "at 15 fps this is 2 seconds". **We serve at 20 Hz, so it's 1.5 s.** Any gap longer than that kills the track, and re-detection mints a new id. Corrected the comment — the tolerance quietly shrank 25% when the sample rate moved and nobody noticed.

Mean keypoint confidence across your three clips runs 0.906 → 0.854 → 0.787, tracking the difficulty: behind a kitchen island, then seated with her back to camera behind a sofa in lamp light. That the occlusion is the cause is inference from the screenshots; the dropout rates are measured.

`MAX_FRAMES` 900 → **12,000** (10 minutes at 20 Hz). Their demo runs on Toyota's own **test split**, on **trimmed** clips with activity boundaries given, same cameras and rooms the model trained on, and it overlays the dataset's **precomputed** LCR-Net poses. That's why it doesn't flicker: nothing is detecting anything live.

Your numbers on Toyota's own split — coarse mean-class **0.7363**, fine 31-class **0.5935** — are in the normal band for skeleton methods. There is real headroom, in this order:

2. **`tv_duration_s` and `drinking_events` will stay 0.00 even with the full ten minutes.** Watching TV while standing is, skeletally, *standing still*; drinking from a mug is a 1.5-second small-object interaction. Neither is recoverable from joints alone — they need RT-DETR in `fuse_objects()`, which is still a stub. ## The television

Both your screenshots have a TV with people on it, and RTMO detects them. A screen in the corner never shares a frame with the room — which makes it look *exactly* like a person who stepped out of detection, so disjoint spans alone would fold it into the resident and attribute a broadcast's motion to her.

The guard is arithmetic, not recognition — and that matters, because `tv_duration_s` and `drinking_events` need RT-DETR, but this doesn't:

> Could one walking person have got from the previous fragment's last box to this one's first box in the gap? At ~1.2 body-heights/second, with one body-height of slack for tracker handoff.

Body-heights because a bounding box's height tracks how tall the person looks, so it needs no camera calibration and no pixels-per-metre guess. In the test: the resident at the counter is 14 body-heights from the TV person with a 4 s gap — unreachable, rejected. The same person re-detected nearby merges, and a walk across the kitchen over 6 s stays reachable.

The slack is deliberately generous, and the reason is asymmetric. Wrongly *splitting* one person re-creates the discarded-activity bug you just had me fix; wrongly *merging* a TV person adds spurious activity that the declared caveat at least covers. So the guard errs toward merging.

This required replacing interval scheduling with longest-path over a DAG — the reachability constraint isn't transitive, so A→B and B→C doesn't imply A→C, and the best chain ending at *i* must consider every compatible predecessor. With single-digit track counts the quadratic scan is free. `track_boxes` now crosses the wire alongside `track_spans`.

I should be straight about the limit: this rejects a TV person by *distance*, not by knowing what a television is. A screen close to the resident would still get through. The real fix is RT-DETR detecting the TV and dropping person boxes inside it — the same work `tv_duration_s` needs, so both land together.
